In [[fluid dynamics]], '''Squire's theorem''' states that of all the [[perturbation theory|perturbations]] that may be applied to a [[shear flow]] (i.e. a [[velocity field]] of the form <math>\mathbf{U} = (U(z), 0, 0)</math>), the perturbations which are least stable are two-dimensional, i.e. of the form <math>\mathbf{u}' = (u'(x,z,t),0,w'(x,z,t))</math>, rather than the three-dimensional disturbances.<ref>[[Philip Drazin|Drazin, P. G.]], & Reid, W. H. (2004). Hydrodynamic stability. Cambridge university press.</ref> This applies to [[compressibility|incompressible flows]] which are governed by the [[Navier–Stokes equations]]. The theorem is named after [[Herbert Squire]], who proved the theorem in 1933.<ref>Squire, H. B. (1933). On the stability for three-dimensional disturbances of viscous fluid flow between parallel walls. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Containing Papers of a Mathematical and Physical Character, 142(847), 621-628.</ref>

Squire's theorem allows many simplifications to be made in [[stability theory]]. If we want to decide whether a flow is unstable or not, it suffices to look at two-dimensional perturbations. These are governed by the [[Orr–Sommerfeld equation]] for [[viscosity|viscous]] flow, and by [[Rayleigh's equation (fluid dynamics)|Rayleigh's equation]] for inviscid flow.
